opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting shifts happening right now. For a long time, the bottleneck in applying machine learning to biology and chemistry has been data. Compared to text or images, we're working with relatively small, noisy, heterogeneous datasets — collected over decades by different labs, under different conditions, often answering questions that weren't designed with machine learning in mind.

What's changing is that we now have technologies that can generate data at scale and with intent. High-throughput screening, automated labs, advances in sequencing, cryo-EM, single-cell methods, DNA-encoded libraries — these let you produce enormous amounts of measurements far more cheaply and consistently than before. And crucially, you can start to design the experiments around what the model needs to learn, rather than just mining whatever happens to exist in the literature.

That creates a really powerful loop. You have models that make predictions about molecular structure, binding, function, and then you can go into the lab, generate exactly the data that tests those predictions or fills the gaps where the model is uncertain, and feed it back in. Over time the model gets better at the parts of chemical and biological space you actually care about. That's quite different from the classical paradigm where computation and experiment sit in separate silos.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the most valuable data isn't always the most voluminous. Generalizing to novel targets or novel chemistry means you need data that covers diversity and captures the underlying physics and biology, not just more examples of things you already understand. So part of the opportunity is being thoughtful about which data to generate: what's going to teach the model something genuinely new.

If you get that right, I think you move from AI as a tool that helps prioritize a few candidates to something much more fundamental, where you can really model and navigate these molecular systems from first principles, and that's when things like drug design start to look radically different.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most exciting things happening right now, and it's a bit underappreciated. If you look at what made the recent wave of AI work, it's really three things coming together: scalable architectures, lots of compute, and crucially, lots of data. In language and vision, the data was essentially already there, sitting on the internet. We got to ride on decades of humans writing text and uploading images.

Biology and chemistry don't look like that. The data that exists is comparatively tiny, it's noisy, it's collected under wildly different conditions by different labs, and a lot of it is trapped in PDFs and supplementary tables. So the naive approach of "scrape everything and train a big model" just runs out of road very quickly.

But what's changed is that the cost and throughput of actually generating new biological and chemical data has dropped dramatically. You've got things like DNA-encoded libraries where you can screen billions of compounds against a target in a single experiment. You've got cryo-EM and the structural data coming out of that. You've got single-cell sequencing, high-content imaging, massively parallel assays where you can test hundreds of thousands of variants at once. And on the chemistry side, automated synthesis and self-driving labs are becoming real.

So the opportunity, as I see it, is that for the first time you can close the loop. You can have a model that not only learns from data but actually decides what data to generate next. That's really the thing I find most interesting, because it turns the data problem from a passive one into an active one. The model proposes experiments, the experiments run at scale, the results come back, and the model improves. You're no longer limited by what happens to be in the literature. You're generating exactly the data you need to reduce the uncertainty that matters for the decision you're trying to make, whether that's finding a binder for a target or predicting a toxicity liability.

And there's a compounding effect here that I think people miss. Every experiment you run isn't just an answer to one question, it's a training signal that makes the next prediction better. So if you build the infrastructure right, where the wet lab and the models are genuinely coupled rather than handing spreadsheets back and forth, the whole system gets smarter over time. That's the flywheel. In language models you can't really do that, you can't ask the internet to produce more of the specific text you need. In biology you can literally go run the experiment.

The challenge, and the reason this is hard rather than just obvious, is that the data has to be designed for machine learning from the start. Consistent protocols, controls, negative results captured and not thrown away, enough diversity that the model actually generalizes rather than memorizing one assay. Most historical data fails on those counts. So I think the real opportunity is less about any single technology and more about the organizations that treat data generation as a first-class engineering problem, built around what the models need to learn, rather than as a byproduct of individual projects. That's where I think the breakthroughs in drug discovery over the next decade are going to come from.

astra-6.text:
I think the really exciting opportunity is to move from learning on the data we happen to have to generating the data we actually need. In biology and chemistry, you can now start to imagine a much tighter loop between an AI model and an experiment. The model makes a prediction, you test it, and that result informs what you do next.

And the key is that you don’t necessarily want to generate more of the same data. You want experiments that distinguish between different hypotheses, that reveal something your model doesn’t yet understand. If you can combine that with increasingly automated, scalable experimental systems, you’ve got a way to actively explore biology and chemistry rather than just analyse existing observations.

That’s exciting because the space of possible molecules and biological interventions is enormous. We’re never going to measure everything. The opportunity is to use AI to make each measurement more informative, and then use those measurements to make the AI better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting opportunity is to create a much tighter loop between generating data and learning from it. In biology and chemistry, you can build models from the data you already have, but those models can also help you decide which experiment to run next. You run that experiment, collect the result, and use it to improve the model.

As those experiments become faster, more automated, and more scalable, you can start to explore that loop much more effectively. The goal isn’t simply to generate more data. It’s to generate the data that helps you answer the scientific question you care about. That creates a really interesting role for AI in guiding discovery.
